claims.text: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 has an fcc random-solid-solution starting structure.
Processing may leave thin oxide layers on the as-built alloy.
At 900°C, 10% H2 in N2 decomposes or chemically modifies the alloy's protective oxide scale.
Loss or modification of oxide-scale integrity permits accelerated hydrogen ingress.
Hydrogen ingress nucleates internal voids and microcracks through hydride formation or localized embrittlement.
High-temperature oxide-scale degradation can be associated with holes, voids, cracks, and scale spallation in high-entropy alloys.
Internal voids and microcracks compromise mechanical integrity and precipitate catastrophic failure under mechanical loading.
Exposure in ambient air at 900°C maintains a continuous and adherent protective oxide scale.
A continuous oxide scale in air retards further oxidation and mechanical damage.
Samples exposed to 10% H2 in N2 will develop internal porosity earlier and to a greater extent than air-exposed samples.
Samples exposed to 10% H2 in N2 will have a higher microcrack density than air-exposed samples.
Samples exposed to 10% H2 in N2 will show measurable hydrogen uptake relative to air-exposed samples.
Reducing-gas exposure will lower load-bearing capacity or fracture toughness and promote earlier crack propagation relative to air exposure.
The proposed governing behavior applies around 900°C for exposure durations up to 100 hours.
Oxide chemistry and morphology in high-entropy alloys depend strongly on oxygen partial pressure and exposure environment.
The relative contribution of hydrogen-induced defects versus oxidation-induced defects remains undetermined.
